The commissions set up under the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act do not report to the government so that the government does not have records giving the names of the persons employed by the commissions. speechtext: Since it requires only three or four weeks to hold a general election in the United Kingdom, is the Prime Minister planning to recommend legislation to shorten the period of time for the holding of a general election in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: SUPPLY OF ELECTRICITY TO INDIAN RESERVES, MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question inquires whether the Prime Minister is planning to recommend legislation to shorten the period of time for the holding of a general election in Canada.
I agree, Mr. Speaker, that it is desirable to shorten the period of time for the holding of a general election in Canada, but a number of steps must be taken before any improvement can be contemplated. Because of very different geographical conditions it may never be possible to be in a position to adopt as short a period as that adopted by the United Kingdom.
In addition to the time required to select enumerators, it now takes 37 days to prepare voters lists, that is to complete enumeration and to print and revise the lists.
Under section 9 of the Representation Commissioner Act which was passed in 1963, the commissioner is required to review, study and report on methods of registration of electors and absentee voting. This study is to get under way after redistribution is in effect and the commissioner, under the law, has two years to complete his study. It is hoped that this study will show that permanent voters lists are feasible, for only then will it be possible to reduce the period of time for the holding of a general election.

Mr. Speaker, the policy of the government has been, where adequate specifications exist, to call for overhaul and repair work to be done on a competitive tender basis. About a year ago the companies engaged in overhaul and repair work for the R.C.A.F. in relation to aircraft instruments-not the aircraft themselves but merely the aircraft instrumentation-were advised that we were now reaching the point where it would be possible to issue specifications to enable competitive tenders to be called. This advice was not only given to the industry but in particular to the four companies engaged in this kind of instrument overhaul work during the previous year.
As a consequence about a year later-and that was some months ago-the overhaul and repair work for instrumentation was divided into three packages. Competitive tenders were called and contracts awarded on this basis. It is estimated that the saving to the government as a result of this competitive arrangement will amount to some $1 million. Further, when four contractors were engaged two of them were American subsidiaries. Now under the new competitive basis only one of the successful tenderers is an American subsidiary.
I would also like to advise the hon. member that we have no information that this change in procedure is going to cause any company to close down.

Increased Cost of Living SUPPLY

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext: that the house go into committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion provides the traditional opportunity to bring matters before the house which, in the opinion of those introducing them, are of first importance and deserve the attention of the house. Also, an amendment may be moved and a vote taken on the amendment. There are a large number of matters which could have been taken up. Various suggestions have been made. Had we proceeded earlier last week, as anticipated, with a motion to go into supply, and the terms of reference had been available to us, it would have been possible to bring before the house the totally inadequate and improper nature of those terms of reference in the matter which has been submitted to Mr. Justice Spence.
We in Her Majesty's loyal opposition do not intend to accept the finality of the terms of reference, which in our opinion were not so framed as to place before the judge the allegations which were made in this house and in respect of which the judge is to make inquiries. However, I make it as clear as I can at once that, while we are not moving an amendment, believing that it would not be appropriate to do so, we do not accept the arbitrary nature of the terms of reference which were determined by the government and formulated in an order in council, and then placed before the house without discussion or consideration of the views of the members of this house.
Having made that clear, I want to bring before the house and the country the general economic situation in the nation as a whole. I particularly want to deal with one phase of the economic situation which affects the people of our nation to a greater extent than any other, and I say that on the basis of mail which I receive.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The two subjects in which people are particularly interested, if one's mail is to be any measure of public feeling, are these. One is the alleged barbarities in the slaughter of seals, and the other is the general position of the average Canadian in the face of a rising and accelerating cost of living. In order to
2942	COMMONS
Increased Cost of Living provide a background for what I have to say in this connection, I point out that there are serious economic difficulties facing this country which have not been met by the government.
It is interesting that today, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) spoke at the Canadian Club in the city of Toronto, he dealt with the difficulties that ministers have in arriving at a consensus of agreement regarding the courses to be taken by cabinet when it meets. We had an example of this the other day, showing the disunity that prevails in the cabinet, when ministers openly were in disagreement with one another, when they could not agree as to what certain legislation meant. That was on March 17. Each minister had a different idea of the meaning of the legislation, and the house ended by providing an adjournment so that they might get together to determine for themselves agreement regarding the legislation, which no one seemed to understand in the same way as another.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said to the persons in the club in the course of his address:
There will undoubtedly be decisions taken by the government, and supported by me, which will cause some concern to many of my friends. The question inevitably arises as to whether one can serve best by trying to work from within the government, or whether he can be more effective and constructive if he has the freedom to express his private views. Every minister undoubtedly wrestles with this conflict from time to time.
I will make reference to that statement a little later on. It is very obvious that the minister, having had several years experience in private business, realizes that some of the measures of the present government cannot be understood by business or anyone else. He made a form of apology in the city of Toronto to those who were present at his meeting today.
Then he goes on to say, after dealing with the high level of economic activity:
The high level of economic activity, stimulated by an extraordinarily large capital program, and coupled with shortages of labour and the difficulty of finding sufficient funds to finance all planned undertakings, will impose inflationary pressures.
This will be one of our most pressing problems as the year advances, particularly having regard to the fact that we experienced an adverse external balance on current transactions in 1965 in excess of $1 billion, and that this figure is apt to be higher in 1966. It will be recalled that the corresponding figure in 1964 was less than one-half billion dollars ($433 million).

DEBATES	March 21. 1966
So the minister goes on. He points out that costs are of importance. Indeed, there are many who are saying today that because of high costs, she is becoming non-competitive in the markets of the world. The minister says that taxes are an important element of costs, and he gives advice-all of which we have endeavoured to give, but our efforts in this regard have fallen on barren soil.
The minister continued to say:
If we are to avoid too great a disparity between our taxes and those of other countries with whom we compete for manpower, capital and markets, the government must be selective in its spending program and resolute in resisting pressures to spend beyond its means.
These are some of the things that we have been saying. He goes on to say that the reason the government voted against the increase to $100 in old age pension was that it was difficult to find revenues to cover current spending. He says, "We would like to have done so." .
It is an interesting speech and it reveals in large measure the effectiveness of the criticism which we levelled at the government. Instead of the political planning promised during the 60 days of decision, proudly paraded as the courageous course to be followed by this government, we have had nothing but forward and retreat, retreat and retreat, from the very beginning of the administration.
Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealt with guide lines. I suggest that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) might study what the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to say in this regard. He goes on:
There were some misunderstandings in interpretation of the intentions of the guide lines and misapprehensions about their impact on the Canadian economy.
Then he goes on:
At the recent meeting-Canadian ministers were assured by the United States authorities that the United States Government was not requesting United States corporations to induce their Canadian subsidiaries to act in any ways that differed from their normal business practices as regards the repatriation of earnings, purchasing and sales policies,-
And so on. Then these general words appear again:
The United States members of the Committee reemphasized the view that United States subsidiaries abroad should behave as good corporate citizens of the country where they are located.
March 21, 1966

Then he says:
Special attention and encouragement should be given to help these companies to adhere to the guiding principles of good corporate citizenship.
Sir, until the opposition pressed for action, the attitude of the government on guide lines was that all was well, despite the fact that Canada was being treated in a way that can only be described as that of an economic beagle-b-e-a-g-l-e.
Now we find the minister saying that the balance of payments problem is a serious matter. The deficit with the United States is rising steadily. We have a deficit which is at an all-time high in peacetime. We have prices, and costs rising. We have Canadian exports being priced out of the markets of the world on account of rising costs. The cost of helping the United States meet its balance of payments problem has been met in part by action that falls on the Canadian consumer; by action that falls on Canadian industry, and on the Canadian manufacturer.
Sir, these are things that we have been saying, while the attitude of the government throughout has been that all was well. One has only to look at the last quarterly balance of payments report to see that the current account deficit with the United States in the third quarter of 1965 had increased $137 million or 11J per cent, over the year before.
You do not see any sign of the government restricting expenditure. They just spend and spend. This government's expenditures are $2 billion higher than ours were at any time. Federal expenditures this year in the main estimates will be $9,318 million. When the supplementary estimates are finally brought in, I am sure that those expenditures will pass the ten billion dollar mark. Last year's expenditures were $8,506 million. If no regard is taken to supplementary estimates that represents an increase of $811 million, or 9J per cent.
That sir, is the general position. Yet the attitude of the government is that all is well. When every person in Canada that I have spoken to is complaining about the high cost of living, with no action being taken by the government, the government's attitude is that all is well.
One of the most interesting articles that I have read, which puts the matter strongly, is an article written by Richard Needham today, in the Globe and Mail, in which he says:
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Take the simple instance of a man who bought a $1,000 Government of Canada bond. This paid him
Increased Cost of Living interest last year of $55 from which income tax (at 25 per cent) took $13.75. That's the official tax. The unofficial tax of inflation was more than twice as high. Consumer prices rose by 2.84 per cent in 1965, meaning the bondholder lost $28.40 on his $1,000 investment. His total tax thus came to $42.15, which, subtracted from his $55 interest, left him with earnings of $12.85, or 1.285 per cent on his investment.
Everywhere the inflation signals are flying. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) with his usual nonchalance laughs about this.
I rise on a question of privilege. I did not laugh about it at all. I simply inquired what happened when hon. gentlemen opposite refinanced the national debt- how much did people lose?

I pointed out the
jocularity. There must have been some reason for it.
These are facts which have been pushed aside by the present government until they must, now, face a serious problem. Across this nation, inflation signals are flying. I will read only briefly from press reports and their headings. From the Financial Post: "Inflation Fires Heat Up Again". This paper asks "Can growth continue without excessive price increases"? That was in December. Major-General R. H. Keefler, according to the Toronto Telegram, in his year end message on December 30, referred to "The upswing which began back in March of 1961". All agree that the upsurge began during the period when we were in office. After speaking of rising labour costs, shortages of skilled labour, price increases and tigher credit, he said:
If allowed to continue unchecked, all this can add up to an alarming price spiral.
Each and every one of these papers has been warning the government. Almost without exception, newspapers throughout Canada have dealt with this problem. The cost of living index is at an all time high. Everywhere attention is called to the danger of our moving into an inflationary period which cannot be controlled and which might easily backfire into a depression. Here is another heading, "Braking Inflation Sharp's Prime Task". This appeared in the London Free Press on January 5. The article says:
In essence, the minister has called for restraint in wage and price increases and urged that the brakes be applied to over-all spending.
Well, that was good advice to others. But what about the government? It has been

March 21, 1966
Increased Cost of Living spending as never before. Nine governments across Canada are spending without correlation. Capital expenditures are multiplying in a way which cannot but lead to ever-increasing inflation. Yet we have a government which declines to take any action.
Here is an article by Bruce Hutchison. No one can ever accuse him of admiring anything more than he admires the present government. This is what he says as reported in the Ottawa Journal of February 26:
The risk, of course, is that we shall price our goods out of the world market when we have a special chance to price them in.
So I could continue.
Yet we have a government which has done nothing about this, though no doubt they will pretend that had they had more time they would have brought measures before the house to deal with these things. But nothing appears on the order paper; nothing has been set down there to meet this problem. The other day we had an example of the ill-digested legislation of which I spoke a moment ago. We had to adjourn with nothing done.
When Mr. Gordon went, everybody felt the excuse he had given, that he had offered the government wrong advice, was only a subterfuge intended to cover up the real reason. But there has been no change in policies.
Let us see what The Economist has to say about this question, and about what the government has done. I read from The Economist of January 1:
Prices moved up a full 3 per cent last year, against a 2 per cent average for the previous four years .... Falling corporate profits, especially in the second half of 1965, could easily trigger further price increases in 1966. Severe shortages of skilled and professional labour take much of the bloom from the employment figures. And the rate of increase in productivity is lagging.
We in Canada have followed the United States. The United States has experienced the greatest expansion in history and, naturally, it affects us. The article goes on to say this about what this government has done.
Beyond Mr. Pearson's fledgling manpower department, and a request last spring for the Economic Council of Canada to study the feasibility of prices and incomes policy (the council has not yet reported), the government has not moved directly to combat the problems of inflation, lagging productivity, and an adverse balance of payments.
That was on January 1. When the election came, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) went across Canada with profligate hand-here a rink and there a rink; no matter what they asked for, they were promised.

No doubt the minister's answer will be: You will have to wait until the budget. This is something which has been going on for months. It is no excuse to say that a budget will be forthcoming and that all will then be well. Action should have been taken earlier. Already the fires of inflation are burning. Many economists fear it will be difficult to put an end to those fires. The housewife, the wage earner, the war pensioner, the old age pensioner, the retired civil servant and all who live on fixed incomes are today facing tremendous increases in the cost of living. It will go still higher in all parts of Canada as one province after another imposes its own sales tax. The value of the dollar is continuing to shrink. Canada as a nation is spending more, and all its people are spending more. The inflationary trend is moving. It is accelerating with the passing months.
We find the prime lending rate increased today by the Bank of Canada from 4f per cent to 51 per cent-the highest figure for many years. The small businessman is virtually loaned out because of tight money. What are the figures? I took the trouble to secure those figures so that there might be no question raised as to their accuracy. Let us look at the record. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) asked the minister a question. He asked what was the cost of living index for the period from January 1, 1965 to December 31, 1965. This was the answer, on the basis of the index in the year 1949 being equal to 100: January, 136.9; February, 137.2; March, 137.3; April, 137.7; May, 138.0; June, 139.0; July, 139.0; August, 139.4; September, 139.1; October, 139.3; November, 140.2; December, 140.8; January, 1966 141.2 and February, 1966, 142.5.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
What does all this add up to? So far as the average Canadian is concerned it adds up to unjustifiable food prices. Everywhere across the nation there has been a cascade of increases in food prices, yet the federal government has not declared a war against inflation.
In 1966 food prices are 6 points higher than they were in January 1965, and everywhere people are asking what is going to be done about this matter. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics in its February 1966 report said the food index in February 1966 was 142.5 points as compared with 133.1 points in February
1965.	Housing was up 3 points in February
1966,	clothing was up 3.8 points, transportation was up 3.7 points, health and personal care were up 4.6 points. These are some of
March 21, 1966

the things of importance to the average person.
What has the government done? The answer is, nothing. True enough, the authority over prices rests with the provinces, but there is action that the federal government could take, and which it has not taken. We cannot accept the excuse, "If you wait until the budget we will do that which we have not done during the last 15 months."
Let me give a few examples. The Ottawa Journal in its issue of Wednesday, March 16, carried advertisements showing the prices of certain foods, and I compare those with the prices which were in effect on March 10, 1965.
During the past few weeks dressed carcasses of pork came down from 45 cents a pound to 32 cents a pound, but nobody knows who gets the advantage. What about the consumer? Has there been any reduction in the price he pays? Let me give some figures at random, and these are not selected to give the proof that there is inflation.
Tomato juice in 1965 was selling at 88 cents for three 48 ounce tins. In 1966 the price is 95 cents. Three 28 ounce cans of tomatoes sold for 88 cents in 1965. Now they are selling at two for 59 cents. In 1965 side bacon cost 69 cents a pound; now it costs 99 cents a pound. Pure pork sausage cost 55 cents a pound in 1965; now it is 65 to 79 cents a pound. Boneless red brand beef roasts, all types, cost 79 cents a pound a year ago; now they cost $1.09 a pound. Steaks were 85 cents a pound, now they are $1.60. Breakfast bacon was 69 cents a pound; now it is 85 cents a pound. Cottage rolls-ham-cost 49 cents a pound in 1965. Today they cost 75 cents a pound. Beef rib roast was 69 cents a pound; now it is 89 cents a pound. Beef rib steak was 79 cents a pound; now it is up to 98 cents a pound. I could give the entire list. Spare ribs cost 52 cents a pound in 1965; now the price is 79 cents a pound. Boneless loin pork roasts were 69 cents a pound in 1965; today the price is 82 cents a pound.
All the way across the board prices are up in one year. Who gets the advantage? The farmer? Not at all. The farmer still continues to receive about the same return for his products.
Oh, the new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) will finish that.

No amount of explanation can account for this tremendous increase

Increased Cost of Living in food costs, with the farmer not receiving additional amounts.
Hear, hear.

There is a great spread between the price the consumer pays and the amount the farmer receives. Fair and reasonable profits are proper. Consideration must be given to the cost of packaging and the like, but there is no explanation which can be given for this great spread. At the same time, as has been pointed out so frequently by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), the prices of farm machinery are mounting.
The Minister of Agriculture went west on his pilgrimage. Not since La Verendrye went out there did anyone receive equal publicity. He said, "You know, when I get back east there is certainly going to be action. I am warning you-there is going to be action." I can just see him when he met with some of his colleagues in the cabinet and they told him, "You are just a new minister. You have ideas, but we don't work that way."
The minister said he was going to have an investigation into the price of farm machinery. What happened to that?
Nothing.

Today, with Lincolnesque calm, when he was asked, "What are you going to do about this" he said, "It is under consideration." The minister does not have to wait for the budget. Let us get an investigation under way and find out the facts.
Another royal commission.

Let us find out who is getting the advantage of this great layer of fat between the price the farmer receives and what the consumer pays, and let us not forget that at the same time the farmer wants to know why his machinery prices are going up, and up, and up. I had great hopes when I read what the Minister of Agriculture said. I thought, well now, we have got a minister; he is going to act. But he was mortified in the presence of the others, and they said no. Then he decided, we can still make the same explanation-"The matter is under active consideration."
Are there combines? Has there been any investigation into this spread? What action has been taken in order to preserve the consumer from these increases? The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) took

March 21, 1966
Increased Cost of Living action in connection with copper and copper products to assure that there would not be shipments abroad. But what action has the government as a whole taken? It started the spiral when it put the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials.
Hear, hear.
Get the date of that and you begin to see it roll. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said he did not believe in that tax.
But he has done nothing about it.

Yes, and when he spoke today in the city of Toronto he said, "After all, don't blame me for anything I did not do, because we in the cabinet cannot do everything we want to do."
What has been done to meet the problem of the fabulous rates charged by some companies on consumer credit? What is being done now? I can only express the hope, so far as the sales tax is concerned, that when the budget comes it will be removed; but if it is, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will then be asking the Liberal party sitting opposite to do that which they voted against only a few weeks ago when we produced our resolution.

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

It has been said that there must be a sharp reduction in government spending, but just before coming into the house I was given an example of public spending on the B and B Commission, which was to settle all our problems in Canada. Well, it sat $3J million worth. Let me give some of the figures in connection with that commission. The staff of the commission now has grown to 225, including 35 who receive more than $10,000 a year. Of the 35 $10,000 a year men, 15 are full time employees. The B and B Commission has 193 full time employees and 32 part time workers. That is just an example of the way they go on. There must be some unified action in this country to deal with inflation. With the responsibility in part constitutionally resting on the provinces, we need a government that will act, a government that will bring together the representatives from the provinces, and together make a concerted attack on inflation which today is the thief that is robbing the average Canadian of his savings, and those on fixed revenues from a fair income.

We need action in the field of agriculture. We asked for action on behalf of the dairy farmers. Nothing is done, but the promise is given that some time action will be taken. When we brought about the devaluation of the dollar, the chief criticism by the present Prime Minister was that that would bring about a great increase in the cost of living, and I have his words here. He complained bitterly, but it did not turn out that way. When we were in office we maintained a level which in no way could be described as inflationary, and that continued throughout the entire period of office.
It is time for agreement-and by agreement I mean a liaison-between the federal and provincial governments on the question of priorities. Everybody is spending, spending as never before. There must be a concerted effort, and this can be brought about only when the federal government once more exerts leadership on behalf of this nation, rather than dissipating its energies in gigantic considerations regarding national unity which have produced disunity.
What happened to the automobile agreement? They boasted about that. They said it was their finest hour. You can almost see them in the position of Sir Christopher Wren, when somebody asked where was his monument. You, sir, know the reply: "I do not know; but, if you would see the monument, look about you." This is the monument: $50 million per year by the removal of excise taxes. Who gets the advantage?
The Liberal party.

Is it the consumer in Canada? Nothing of the kind. You would have thought when they entered into the agreement they would have made arrangements whereby Canadians would be able to have their cars reduced in price. But what a business! These companies export to the United States, are able to compete over there against United States prices, and at the same time Canadians are paying through the nose. Is there any wonder, with a government that will not act, that the cost of living continues to go up and up?
Sir, we tried to bring about a reduction in taxes, but on our motion, which I mentioned a moment ago, in respect of building materials and production machinery, they voted against us. We ask that action in this regard be taken. What about the old age pension? Well, an old age pensioner has written to me in respect of the $75 monthly in the old age
March 21, 1966

pension, which was started in October, 1963. Since the cost of living and price index has jumped, the $75 monthly now has a purchasing power of $70.20. It has lost $4.80 in the intervening months with the added cost of living.
Now, the government is flying another kite. They voted against the $75 a month, and they have had a lot of criticism over that. When the Minister of National Health and Welfare went west, he said the Senate proposal would provide for a basic guaranteed minimum income at age 65. He said the Senate proposal would prove less burdensome on taxpayers, and the Senate plan he said would correct a major anomaly in the old age pension program-the paying of higher pensions to persons who do not need such assistance.
Then in the next couple of days the Minister of Agriculture made another pilgrimage. He went to the Prime Minister's constituency and he let the people know this had an appeal. Well, everybody wants to see benefits being assured to the older people of our country. But, such a somersault on the part of the government. A few weeks ago when I mentioned $100 a month, they said no. Every last one of them voted against it; and now under the pressure of public opinion and with recognition of the effect that the rising cost of living is having, suddenly they forget who it was who gave consideration to the plight of the old age pensioner.
In addition to that, what about the war pension; what about the retired civil servants who have been denied anything whatever from this government? Mr. Speaker, we in this party have been urging the government for the past three years to give some measure of protection to the Canadian consumer. We live in a pluralistic society, in which various groups are able to band themselves together for their common protection. The manufacturers are well organized, as are the financial institutions, the life insurance companies, the banks and all the other various groups are well organized. They have organs to express their points of view and they have lobbies to present their opinions to the government.
Other groups are not so well protected. Labour is about 25 per cent organized. Those who are organized are able to bargain with some degree of success. However about 75 per cent are not able to bargain, and usually their wages lag behind both the rising cost of living and increased productivity. Farmers, as I have already pointed out, have virtually no bargaining power. Because their product is perishable, they must sell it when it is ready for market. They have no way of withholding their produce from market, and consequently the price which they have received for their produce has always lagged behind the cost of production.
But the most defenceless group in our society are the consumers. They stand naked

If one compares the cost of living percentage points for 1945 with those of today, one sees that family allowances no longer meet the purposes for which they were granted in 1945.
We of the Ralliement Creditiste support wholeheartedly and completely those statements and comments made by the hon. member. I do not believe I could be accused of boasting if I say that we have been the champions and promoters of those claims. As a matter of fact, we have never stopped asking, and we never will, that family allowances be increased in keeping with the rise in the cost of living.
Mr. Speaker, far be it from me to doubt the sincerity of the remarks made by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska, who is an honourable citizen and a good father, but over the five years since his party came into office, what have they actually done to show that they meant what they said about increasing family allowances?
Every day, I get at my office requests asking the government to increase family allowances to $25 a month per child, and that up to 21 years of age. To prove what I am saying, I will read right now two resolutions sent to me by the voters in the northern region of my riding.

Pearson, asking all Canadian citizens to reduce their living expenditures by 25 per cent to further the country's economic recovery, we strongly suggest that it would be logical and more humane to distribute a dividend of $25 per month at least to each Canadian citizen out of the production surplus accumulated each year by Canadians, instead of giving that same surplus to foreign countries as all our governments have done since confederation.

Copy of that second resolution was sent to the Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Lester
B.	Pearson.
For most hon. members in this house, it seems utopic that the people who signed the resolution I have just read should ask for the distribution of a dividend of $25 per month at least to each citizen of Canada out of the production surplus accumulated each year by Canadians. Well, it is not so; those people know what they are saying and, most of all, they know what they want. Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to bolster their claims with figures which will certainly test seriously the sincerity of the too numerous promises which are made at election time.
In the 1960, the national production was $36 billion; five years later, that is in 1965, that national production had reached $51 billion and consumption stood at $36 billion only. Consequently, there is a $15 billion surplus between national production and the national consumption. It is out of this surplus that we demand a $25 monthly dividend for every Canadian citizen.
Let us stop asking if there are still poor people in fabulously rich Canada. There lies utopia, the disparity between so much poverty amid such wealth.
Much has been said about the social problems of poverty, misery and economic uncertainty in Canada lately. Heads of families should receive a graduated salary according to the number of dependant children, or adequate family allowances to allow for their increased expenditures, without depriving their families. Officials, gravely discussing poverty, being paid $25,000 a year, are barely qualified to express their views on the problem; the workers should be consulted instead.
As far as those well-fed people who claim that poverty is the result of drink, laziness or lack of ambition, this is sheer hypocrisy, self-righteousness and cowardice.
There may be drunkards, loafers and people easily satisfied among the poor of course,

but they are in minority and most would wish for an easier life for themselves and for their families. Many are sober and hardworking. And drunkenness and idleness have many more practitioners among the rich living off the poor, and often they have climbed not through ambition but through sheer luck, if not through dishonesty and political patronage.
The true causes of poverty, misery and insecurity are low wages, chronic unemployment due to repeated lay-offs, employment difficulties constantly increased, all because of the greed of the big companies and of the incompetence of the government and of well-fed high officials.
I need no other proof than what the Auditor General states in his annual report to the Government for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1965. This report is truly a "plank".

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments respecting the amendment, and the amendment to the amendment, which have been moved this afternoon. Before doing so I want to say one or two words in reference to the opening remarks of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
The right hon. gentleman suggested in opening this debate that in so far as the members of his party are concerned, they would not accept the disposition of the Munsinger case which occupied so much of the time of this house a few days ago. He suggested that they would not accept the terms of reference contained in the order in council, as well as a number of other things. I am not particularly interested in whether or not the Leader of the Official Opposition and his party accept the terms of reference, but I am concerned about what they intend to do with this whole matter at some time in the future.
I think it is their right and privilege to bring this matter back into the House of Commons whenever they choose to do so, because of the provisions in our rules which allow members to raise a question of privilege at any time they feel they have been abused or aggrieved by statements made either inside or outside this house. Having acknowledged that right I hope, if and when they do bring this matter back into the House of Commons, they will introduce it in a procedurally correct way so that there will be a motion before the house and some determination made of the debate and the consequences of that debate.
I must agree with the Leader of the Opposition that referring this whole matter to a judicial inquiry does not settle the alleged question of privilege referred to several days ago, because such an inquiry does not have the right to consider such a question of privilege. That is all I wish to say on that subject, Mr. Speaker.
In dealing with the matters now before the house, namely the amendment and the amendment to the amendment, it would be well for us to bear in mind that the concern expressed in those amendments and felt by hon. members of this house is felt by a large
Increased Cost o/ Living part of the Canadian population, and is similar to the concern which was felt about exactly this same matter in 1957. I have before me a page taken from the Financial Post of March 9, 1957. Under the headline "Inflation and Credit: The Great Debate", this article refers to whether there should be an easing or tightening in the credit and money supply, and it states:
The current debate about tight money is generating more heat among businessmen than any government policy for a long time.
The article then gives some explanations about the kind of arguments which monetary authorities would probably advance in favour of their policies.
At this time we are in a position where we can review in retrospect what happened when Canadians were concerned about inflation and the tightening or easing of money at that time. We can also review the consequences of the actions that were taken. In this regard we should bear in mind the shotgun measures suggested by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) to deal with this matter of tight or easy money during an inflationary period, and the undesirable side effects which accompanied those measures and lasted for longer than most of us in this country wanted.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Certainly we do not want a repetition of the consequences that flowed from the action of the government and the Bank of Canada in 1960, 1961 and 1962, because in those years we had the highest level of unemployment in Canada since the end of the second world war. Therefore if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and his advisers intend to use exactly the same kind of measures to meet the situation that faces us today, I hope they will also bear in mind the consequences of those measures.
I agree with many of the statements that have been made this afternoon. I agree with the statement that there is a regrettable increase in the cost of living and in certain commodities. There is no question at all in our minds about that. But I believe we also have the responsibility to examine in detail what has been the cause of the situation in which we find ourselves today. One of the most popular reasons given in the last few weeks for the increased cost of living is that the price of food has gone up.
If you look at the latest Dominion Bureau of Statistics report-and this report has been
March 21, 1966

Increased Cost of Living referred to a number of times today-you will find that from February, 1965, to February, 1966, there was an increase in the consumer price index for all items from 137.2 to 142.1. If you look at the increase for the single item "food" from February, 1965, to February, 1966, you find that it went up from 133.1 to 142.5. Therefore there is no argument but that there has been a greater increase in the single item "food" than any other item included in the consumer price index.
Statements have been made that perhaps the reason for this is that farmers are getting more money for the food they produce; that is, the raw material that goes into the groceries. Before that suggestion is accepted by any member of this house or the Canadian public generally, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be well for us to examine whether there has been an increase in the amount received by the food producers in the country which corresponds with the increase in the consumer price of food.
If you look at the situation in the early 1950's or 1949-that year, by the way, is the basis for the consumer price index, 1949 equalling 100-you will find that many of the major commodities that enter into the category of food, such as beef and pork, commanded for the farmers a price as high as that they receive today. Let us take beef for example. In 1950, 1951 and for part of 1952 the price of beef to the farmer was actually higher than it is today. That is, the price of live steers, or whatever grades they choose to sell beef in the marketplace, was higher in those days than it is in 1966. I shall say a few more words about that later.
In so far as pork is concerned, in those years the price of hogs taken to market by farmers was actually higher than it is today. Yet in the period 1949 to February, 1966, we find that the price of food has risen 42.5 per cent. The point I am trying to make, Mr. Speaker, is that while the price the consumer pays for food has increased some 42 per cent during the last 16 years or so, there has been no increase at all to the farmer in respect of many of the major commodities that enter into the price of food. Let us take wheat for example. The price of wheat was almost as high in those years as it is today, as far as the farmer is concerned. Therefore something has to be examined other than the price level being paid to the farmers for producing food.


I am interested in the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). It says:
"and this house further regrets that the government has not established a Prices Review Board to determine the extent to which price increases are unjustified and to take appropriate steps to reduce such prices accordingly."
I believe that we need a prices review board as the hon. member has suggested, but I also believe that quite apart from setting up any new boards the government has not taken all the action it could have taken under the Combines Investigation Act. I do not think it is necessary to go into a great deal of detailed explanation in this respect, because I believe it is well known that the distribution of food in Canada is gradually but constantly being concentrated in fewer and fewer hands. In other words, the supermarkets which distribute food are not only falling into the hands of fewer and fewer people but we have seen a tremendous increase in so-called "vertical integration" in the distribution of food.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Supermarkets and retail stores that used to buy from wholesale establishments, which in turn made their purchases of the raw materials and even in some cases processed those materials, are gradually disappearing and the whole operation almost from the primary production right through to the distribution to the ultimate consumer is now being carried out by the same corporations and companies. I think there needs to be an investigation in this regard. I think the combines investigation authorities already have sufficient authority, if you want to call it that, to look into these matters, and I believe they should be looked into. A few months ago the price of wheat went down anywhere from 10i cents to 20 cents a bushel; I think it averaged something like 13 cents a bushel. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam pointed out that there was no reduction in the price of a loaf of bread or any other bakery product. Yet when the price of wheat has again risen to almost the same level it was about a year and a half ago, then, as I noticed in the paper very recently, one baker suggested the increased cost of flour was the major contributing factor in his over-all cost which gave him justification for increasing the price of his bread. Surely if there is no justifiable cause for lowering the price of consumer goods when the price of wheat goes down, there should not be justification for increasing the
March 21, 1966	COMMONS
price of bread by the same amount when the price of wheat goes up. Yet this is exactly what is happening in the consumer price scale today, and these are the reasons being advanced for this action.
Let us look at the price of pork for a moment. It is true that the price the farmers receive in the marketplace for pork or hogs has gone up substantially in the last two years. There is no question of that, and I do not disagree with it because I think about two years ago the selling price was below the cost of production. There has been at least a corresponding or perhaps more than a corresponding increase in the price of pork and pork products to the consumer.
During the last few days the price of hogs in the marketplace has gone down. I received a letter this morning from Calgary which advised me that in the marketplace there the price of hogs has gone down from a high of 41 cents per pound three weeks ago to around 30 cents per pound today for the same carcasses. But there has been no corresponding decrease in the price of bacon or pork or any other pork products at the retail level.
Therefore I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will take cognizance of these price movements to consumers, and that he will look very carefully at the corresponding price movements of the products of the primary producers. I hope he will also have the combines investigation authorities take a look at the movement of prices at the consumer level and at least try to investigate the people involved in the distribution and processing of food to see whether they are engaging in some unconscionable profit-taking along with these price movements.
Looking ahead a little, Mr. Speaker, we are, as many of your members have indicated, concerned about inflation and the increased price of consumer goods, particularly food. However, it seems to me that the problem will be looming again in the future and that it will get worse instead of better, according to some of these other statistics which are available.
For example, in a Dominion Bureau of Statistics report on credit dated March 1966, the following appears. I am not going to read all these figures because this report is a matter of public record and anyone can look it up. But it indicates in relation to finance companies dealing with the financing of consumer goods that there has been a 10.1 per cent increase in the amount of credit outstanding for consumer goods. The small loans companies show an increase of 13.2 per cent in their outstanding credit, and instalment credit from these small loan companies has gone up 24.1 per cent. In addition to that, credit outstanding on the books of department stores has gone up 11 per cent. Furniture and appliance stores show an increase of 4 per cent. Fully secured personal loans from chartered banks have gone up 18 per cent, and other loans 21.9 per cent.
This would indicate, Mr. Speaker, that there must be a shortage of effective purchasing power in the country to buy goods and services that we as a nation have produced. Because if it is necessary for the consumers of Canada not only to spend all of their disposable income but also during the course of one year to increase the amount of credit required for their purchases, then they have mortgaged their incomes for the future. Somewhere down the road they are going to need not only their disposable income, if I may use that term, to buy all these goods, but they will also have to pay back some of this consumer credit which has been extended to them by these financial institutions. So, Mr. Speaker, I think we would only be fooling ourselves if we looked at these figures and concluded that the situation is going to get better in the near future.
In so far as the prices review board and increased activity by the combines investigation branch is concerned, I should like the house to know that we in this party believe in free enterprise. But more than that, Mr. Speaker, we believe in free competitive enterprise. I do not believe that you can have free enterprise in the truest sense of the word unless there is competition. Therefore, when we talk of free enterprise the word "competitive" is extremely important, because enterprise is free no more without competition.
I also think there is justification for the federal government to look into the matter of food distribution to determine whether or not there is effective competition in the processing and distribution of food. If there is, and if they can prove that there is, then you would have to transfer some of the responsibility for increased food prices to customer demand. If the customers want food packaged and processed in more expensive and fancier wrappers and they are willing to pay for it, then

But if, as I suggested, agreements have been arrived at between the fewer and fewer number of people involved in food distribution with regard to some kind of pricing, then such would be a valid case for the combines investigation authorities to look into.
When we are trying to find solutions to these problems, in addition to setting up a prices review board-or whatever is the method used-to look into price differentials, perhaps the government should also look very carefully at its own expenditures. I know there has been some action taken by the government to postpone some of its own building programs because the price of construction has greatly advanced during the past few months, and I think we in this party would, to a degree at least, support that sort of action. I know that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works are well aware that there has been an unusually rapid increase in the cost of construction during the past few months. We agree with this measure, provided it is done on a selective basis and provided there is not a cut-back in government construction in areas where there really is not a severe employment problem. Where there is still some unemployment, these project should go ahead.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have also to look at the expansion of all government services. We must also look at areas where government services are a substitute for services previously paid by individuals. Perhaps this area is not so dangerous, so far as affecting inflationary pressures is concerned, but when one looks at the expansion of government spending from, for example, 1956 to 1966, he sees that one of the greatest increases in government spending has been in the matter of public debt charges. The Minister of Finance will be well aware that the estimates in the blue book for 1956 contained an item of $456 million for the total interest charges on the whole national debt, and that this year those charges for the same item are well over $1 billion.
One cannot blame the present Minister of Finance for all that increase, because I suppose the greatest upswing in these charges came about in the now famous conversion loan of 1958 which recalled a lot of bonds that had not matured, which were then reissued for a substantially higher rate of interest.

We in this party do not mind the government's meeting its obligations so far as bonds are concerned; but it seems to me unjustifiable to call back several billions of dollars worth of bonds on contracts that had been issued, and then offer a 50 per cent increase in the earning power of those bonds even before they had matured.
I suggest to you, sir, that the government's action respecting its handling of the public debt over the past ten years has been at least one of the major contributing factors to the whole increase in the cost of production and to the cost of living in Canada.
We hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government is not going to proceed with what has been termed a shot-gun solution to this matter of inflation. As has been pointed out, there are areas in this country which are not overextended in the economic field. We hope that the government will use the authority it talked about a while ago with respect to the mobility of workers, to help transfer manpower from certain areas to other areas of greater economic activity, so that workers transferred could be used in those areas of greater employment opportunity.
In the areas where there is a problem, government action will have to be taken to move workers into areas where they may be employed. I think it is fair to say that in Alberta and British Columbia, and perhaps other places, particularly in Toronto and Montreal, there is really not any unemployment at the moment. In fact in some areas there is a very severe labour shortage. In those areas I have mentioned there is a severe shortage of labour in agriculture; there is a severe shortage of labour in most of the professional groups, and in most of the construction occupations. Therefore, when the minister says that he is not going to put the brake on the economy, but that it is necessary to try to find a balance to control inflationary pressures without causing a depression or recession, we agree with him.
In some areas, Mr. Speaker, we do not agree with the minister. We were unable to select any positive steps that the Minister of Finance intended to use, to try to keep inflationary pressures down, and at the same time not put the brake on our whole economy.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I just wish to re-emphasize that we, in this party, would like the members of this house to know and the general public of Canada to know that this increase in the cost of living has not been
March 21, 1966

reflected in a corresponding increase of income to the farmers of this country, in producing food over the last five years.
We also want the Minister of Finance to know that we are going to support him if he can come forward with some action that will in fact keep our economy going at a very high level, at the same time take some selective action, if I may put it that way, to hold back in some areas where perhaps there is too much heat with respect to economic activity.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say to the Leader of the Opposition, when he suggested that we voted against an increase in the pensions, that we keep hearing a repetition of the same charge every time a debate of this nature comes up.
It must hurt.

Of course the truth of the matter is that in January we voted on a motion of non-confidence. All members of this house who want to be honest with themselves and to know anything about the rules in this house-
Oh, no.

-know that the wording of the non-confidence motions in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, or of motions amending the motion that the house resolve itself into committees of supply, do not mean anything in terms of what the consequences of supporting these motions would be.
You protest too much.
If the Leader of the Opposition wants to go on trying to keep this from the Canadian people, that is his business.
Methinks thou doth protest too much.
You may think I protest too much, but I think every time some of the members of this house try to deceive the Canadian people, it is the responsibility of those of us who want to be honest-
Hear, hear.
-to repeat and to state the facts and the effects surrounding the consequences of those kinds of motions.

How would you vote if the government had a majority?
A good question.

The responsibility for the opposition to assist the government to govern the country would not be so great if they had a majority, and hon. members to my right know that very well.
Now that we have had this little review of the rules and discussed some of the technical possibilities I think we had better return to what is practical. I think this debate is useful. I believe the subject matter raised by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) pointing to this inflationary pressure has initiated a very useful discussion and I hope hon. members in all parties in all corners of the house will get on their feet and make positive suggestions to the Minister of Finance, suggestions which they will spell out and which they will support, for dealing with this very serious problem now facing the Canadian people.

Without intervening too far in the discussion we have just had on the rules one thing should be noted. The question whether one votes for a motion because of what appears on the surface or because of what lies underneath is an academic one. But I should like to point out to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat that whereas his group supported the government in connection with old age pensions, not so very long ago the Liberal party supported the Social Credit group in connection with debt free money. I think things are just about even, whether the purpose was so obvious or not.

Could I ask the hon. member a question? If we had voted otherwise in that particular instance would it have

brought about an increase in old age pensions for the people?
I would think so.
A dream.

Surely we do not have sham battles in this house. Had the house expressed itself as being in favour of an increase in old age pensions I believe the government would have had either to resign or to increase the pensions. The decision would have been one for the government to take, but the expression of opinion by the house would have been loud and clear; the government would have been obliged to act or to resign.
The most serious problem facing the average Canadian today is the constant increase in the cost of living. This applies whether a person is living on a fixed income or not. Admittedly the effects of inflation are felt more severely by those who are living on fixed incomes, whose hard earned savings dissolve as the cost of living rises. The dollar earned and saved in earlier years as a unit of real value in exchange for the necessities of life now brings less and less. A few years ago, we called such an increase "galloping inflation". That is a horse and buggy term and I think that inflation would in this modern age be better described as "jet propelled." The comparison is a good one, because the recent figures show it to be just that.
When we look at the figures for the cost of living for the month of February over the past ten years we see a dramatic increase. This is a situation which must be dealt with quickly if the economy of the country is not to suffer a serious blow. In February, 1955, the cost of living equalled 116.3; in 1956 it was 116.4; in 1957, it was 120.5; in 1958 it was 123.7; in 1959, it was 125.7; in 1960, it was 127.2; in 1961, it was 128.9; in 1962, it was 129.8 and in 1963 it was 132.00.
This represents a fairly constant and small annual increase of one or two points a year. In 1964, however, it goes up to 134.5 and in 1965, to 137.2-an increase of almost three points. And in 1966 it was 142.1, an increase of almost five points. This is a dramatic and most discouraging increase. As a rule I do not like to make comparisons but I think there is one I should make. In the five years from 1958 to 1963 during which a Conservative government was in power the cost of living increased by 8.3 points. In the three years since the present government took over, from

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
And you were right.

March 21, 1966
Increased Cost of Living

The effect of this failure is that the benefit from our social welfare legislation, as passed in previous and in recent years, is lost. What is the use of increasing pensions, salaries and welfare benefits if the result is a smaller purchasing power because of inflation and higher taxes?
The spiral of higher living costs, more wages, and higher production costs also affects our selling power abroad. The dollar devaluation, which was a powerful tool in increasing our foreign markets and reducing our imports, now is being offset completely by higher cost of production in Canada, with the result that our power to compete in foreign markets is being eaten away. This is proven very conclusively by our export-import figures.
According to a Dominion Bureau of Statistics release of March 11 this year, commodity imports into Canada in 1965 increased 15.4 per cent or $1,150 million over 1964. Our exports, however, were up only 5.6 per cent or $461 million over 1964. I should mention that this export figure includes the large grain shipments without which our commodity exports would be pathetic. In the result, in 1965 we lost $689 million in our foreign trade in respect of commodities. We must ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker, to what do we attribute this loss?
I submit that inflation undoubtedly has a major part in it. Inflation increases the cost of production and thereby reduces our power to compete in foreign markets. I should like to turn for a moment to the attitude of the government in connection with the problems related to inflation. I think it generally is accepted that spending alone has a great effect on the question of inflation. We can look to the government itself to see what the picture is with regard to its spending while it has been in office. I have taken some figures from two books of estimates which are on record. The first is the book of estimates for the year 1962-1963, the last year in which the former Conservative government was in office; the second is the current estimates for 1966-67 which are the projected spending of the present government.
Total government spending in 1962-63 amounted to $6,276 million. In the current estimates the total is $7,950 million. This is a tremendous increase in spending on the part of the government itself which gives the example to others who are following the lead of the government.

I also picked out a few of the departments in which there have been dramatic increases in spending. I will admit that perhaps there may be differences in circumstances over these few years, but I have taken examples which are most dramatic and which I think at least have equivalent value. The estimates of the Civil Service Commission, for example, in 1962-63 show a figure of $4,815,000; for the coming year they are estimated at $8,087,000. That is a very large increase. As we go away from the wartime era and as the Department of National Defence is making an effort to reduce expenditures, we would also expect that the Department of Defence Production would be cutting back, but we find that while this department in 1962-63 spent almost $19 million, the projected spending for 1966-67 is $26 million. This is another dramatic increase. This does not include the Department of Industry which has the same minister. In
1962-63 there was no department and there was no spending, but for 1966-67 the Department of Industry has estimated expenses of $50,582,000. That is a new department and a new additional expenditure. In 1965-66 the projected estimate for this department was $36 million.
Many of us wonder about these two departments, Defence Production and Industry, Mr. Speaker. Are they really giving value for the tremendous sums of money which are being spent? Many people seriously doubt that value is being received. They have not yet seen, and many people in industry really do not expect to see, the value of this department in relation to its spending. If the question of exports and imports has anything to do with it, the picture is much the reverse, because I am going to show in a minute that our balance in commodities has decreased this year by a large figure, $680 million, over the previous year. Therefore, if the increased spending of $50 million in the Department of Industry has done anything it certainly has not increased our commodity exports.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I also looked at the Post Office expenditures. In 1962-63 they were $192 million; in 1966-67, they are $252 million. Where is the additional expenditure justified? I do not know. There have been increases in postal rates but the deficit seems to be increasing. Is this the result of bad management or an improper attitude toward the whole problem of increased spending and inflation?
The increases in the estimates for the Department of the Secretary of State have

me absolutely baffled. In 1962-63 the expenditures of that department were $5 million. The estimated expenditures for this year are $45 million. I appreciate that a portion of that results from a special statute but there is still an increase in the normal operating expenditures, being the difference between $5 million and $17,500,000.
As I have said, these increases in government spending are indicative of a careless attitude and an absolute lack of concern on the part of this government for the cost of government and the question of inflation generally.
In comparing the spending totals appearing in the estimates for the year 1962-63 with the current spending totals one can see there has been an increase of 25 per cent in that four year period, whereas during the same period the cost of living increased 9.5 per cent. Perhaps to be fair we should only look at the past three year period, from 1963 to 1966, during which the cost of living index has risen from 132 points to 142 points, an increase of ten points with a percentage increase of 9.3. This would indicate that the spending increase is roughly 25 per cent and the cost of living increase is 9.3 per cent. Therefore the government is spending at a rate of increase in excess of the cost of living increase. One can only assume that the government is thereby contributing to the spiralling cost of living rather than slowing it down. The government's spending has increased at a greater rate than even the tremendously increasing cost of living.
We have seen no evidence that the government is concerned about holding prices down. I can remember that in the 1956-57 period, when I was first running for election to this house, one of the most serious problems then being discussed was price increases and the related fact that producers were not getting a fair share of the increase while the consumer was paying more. The cost-price squeeze, as it was referred to then, was a major issue in the election of 1957, certainly so far as the rural areas were concerned. We have not heard very much about this situation in the past few years but it is beginning again to be of importance. Once more the cost-price situation is beginning to squeeze the farmers on one side, who are not getting increased prices, and the consumers on the other side, who must pay more for their goods.
I think some of the causes of this situation are the increased cost of administration, the
Increased Cost of Living increased cost of government and the increased cost of production. The cost of processing goods is once again out of control. It is no longer in the position it was for the past number of years during which fair prices were being received by producers while at the same time consumer prices were rising at a slow rate.
Just before the adjournment at six o'clock I pointed out that the cost of living in the past three years had increased ten points compared with an increase of only eight points during the previous five year period when the Conservative government was in power. I think this is something the people of this country should consider. Why is the cost of living becoming so high and why is the government apparently taking no action in this regard?
We are continually told that when the budget comes down we will perhaps be given answers to some of these questions. I hope the government can do something by legislation to alleviate this situation, but legislation is not necessarily the answer. In my view the real problem is related to the attitude taken by the government as exemplified not only through legislation but through administrative and executive action. It is my firm belief that this government has gone ahead with expenditures without making any effort to control the increase in the cost of living and that they have been very careless in this regard. Legislation placed on the statute books will not reverse an attitude displayed by the government.
The public is very quick to grasp such an attitude. The business community and everyone else grasp and understand an attitude on the part of the government which indicates that it is either trying to keep the lid on inflation and keep things under control or that no effort is being made to do this at all. It does not matter what legislation is passed, what the budget indicates or what we are asked to approve in the way of tax measures. These will not remedy the basic problem of this government, which is the result of careless spending and a careless attitude toward general cost increases.
I suggest finally that the answer to our present economic problem does not lie in legislative measures. Nor will it be found in budgetary measures. The answer can only be found if this government turns away from the easy answers and stops doing things on a helter-skelter basis because it feels it might

It is my belief, Mr. Speaker, that this government must set a steady course and maintain it, giving the people of Canada the assurance that they are doing something toward controlling inflation and expenditure, setting an example which others in Canada can follow in maintaining fair increases in the cost of living. We realize that there has been an increase in the cost of living each year for a number of years. The Canada pension plan was based on a presumption that the cost of living would increase. It was assumed that the cost of living would increase at the rate of 2 per cent per annum and that wages would increase at the rate of 3 per cent per annum. On this assumption the Canada pension plan was devised to cover a built-in increase in pensions. That is satisfactory to the extent that it may provide some protection to old age pensioners, but it is indicative of the attitude of this government that this increase is inevitable. Such an attitude can only lead to a belief on the part of the people of the country that excessive spending is the order of the day and that with this government we cannot expect anything more than a continued and continual increase in the cost of living.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house deals with inflation. Rising prices are always a problem. They are more of a problem in an economy such as that of Canada at the present time, namely, an economy approaching full employment. A few years ago when the economy was not expanding, when it was relatively stagnant, prices rose, but they rose relatively slowly at a rate of around 1 per cent to 2 per cent a year. In the last two or three years we have seen increases of the order of 2 per cent and latterly 3 per cent. This rate is becoming excessive. The answer is difficult, as I said before. We want, above all, full employment. We want to use all our factories and employ all our manpower. How do we manage prices under these circumstances? This is a burning question not only in countries like Canada but in many countries overseas which throughout most of the post-war period have been struggling with the serious problem of inflation. Their prices have been rising more rapidly than ours.

The question to which we must address ourselves in this house, however, is not so much the identification of the problem, because we admit to rising prices, but the solution of the problem. I contend that a number of steps have already been taken by the government which will help to moderate the rise in prices and I want this evening to advocate one or two others which I think could be pursued with a little more energy by the government in order to contain prices more effectively.
I should like to deal particularly with trade. By that I mean freer trade, because I think through international competition, indeed through competition internationally and domestically, we could help to contain prices.
First, however, I should like to refer to a recent report produced by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development in Europe, the O.E.C.D. It is a report on Canada. It was released in December, 1965, and has several interesting things to say which I think might usefully be put on the record. At the very outset it states that in Canada "economic activity has been expanding very rapidly in recent years".
The report says:
Economic activity has expanded very rapidly in recent years, mainly stimulated by growing exports and gross fixed asset formation. Unemployment has fallen well below 4 per cent and capacity utilization rates have been raised. On the whole the pressure of demand would not seem to be excessive, and the rise in prices, although accelerating somewhat, generally remains moderate-
This is the view of the economists employed by the O.E.C.D. looking at Canada in a sequence of surveys which examined the economies of other countries as well. The
O.E.C.D. report goes on to say:
In Canada, as in the United States, the expansion that began early in 1961 has now lasted for nearly five years, longer than any previous peacetime upturn in economic activity. Following some signs of slowdown in the middle of 1962, the expansion accelerated in 1964 and continued at a high rate in 1965. Indeed, since the middle of 1963-
Incidentally, that is when this administration took office.
-activity has been expanding rather faster than in the United States and most European member countries.
The report goes on to examine the principal forces for expansion in the country, forces which also tend to increase prices. One is the remarkable increase in new investment by private enterprise. Another is the remarkable increase in exports. In other words,
March 21. 1966	COMMONS
exports, including exports not only of raw materials but highly manufactured products, together with new investment have been the two major factors tending to increase prices. Several hon. members during the debate today, including the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), have castigated the government for excessive expenditure. I should like to read a short paragraph from the O.E.C.D. report dealing with government expenditure. It says:
Government expenditure on goods and services in real terms has increased less rapidly than real (gross national product) -
In other words, government expenditure has not been growing as rapidly as national production and income. The report goes on to say that the provinces and municipalities account for most of the expansion. Government spending has been growing, though not as rapidly as the economy, and the growth is attributable almost entirely to expanded outlays of the provinces and the municipalities. The report concludes that particular paragraph with these words:
The increase in federal expenditure has mainly consisted of transfer payments.
Transfer payments are payments out of federal taxation to the provinces for the conduct of business which falls within the constitutional responsibility of the provinces. Therefore I think we see from this report, first, an indication that the Canadian economy is growing very rapidly; second, that prices, while they are increasing are certainly not out of control; third, that our performance relative to other countries is quite good and, fourth, that government outlays, particularly federal government outlays, are not a major cause of inflation in this country.
I wish also to refer briefly to the second annual review of the Economic Council of Canada which discusses the question of prices on page 24. It says:
In recent years, prices and costs have advanced much less rapidly in the United States and Canada than in overseas industrial countries.
This should be reassuring to us and particularly reassuring to our export industries. There are various solutions which a government can employ to solve the problem of rapidly rising prices, prices rising at a rate of 3 per cent a year or more. One is increased taxation; another is a ceiling on its own expenditures. But other measures have been taken by the present administration and I 23033-188
