speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
We must emphasize increased productivity. By this I mean increased output through the more efficient use of manpower. Essentially this means through new plants, new processes and new techniques, better utilization of labour, higher capital investment in plant and equipment. This is one of the principal objectives of the Department of Industry. This is one of the main reasons for its formation and I suggest that already in its young life-it is only about two years old-it has done a remarkable job in this respect.
Productivity is one thing. Other things are greater mobility, particularly greater mobility of our people and greater ease of movement of new funds for investment in new industries. These are also important factors which can help to contain cost and price increases. We need a more flexible economy. I believe we need a more open economy. We need a more research-conscious economy. Various measures have been introduced in the last three budgets aimed at increased expenditure on research and development. The main burden of my remarks, however, will have to do with trade.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
As I said earlier, I believe that in circumstances where we have relatively full employment we also have the best of all possible circumstances in which to reduce trade barriers, in which to cushion the impact of foreign competition on people who will have to change their jobs and perhaps even change the locality in which they live. Full employment cushions the impact of competition on old plants, plants which will either have to be re-equipped and enter into new lines of production or plants which may have to go out of business entirely. These are the best possible circumstances, with relatively full employment, in which to engage in this process

March 21, 1966
Increased Cost of Living of reducing tariffs and eliminating protection, particularly the protection of industries which are no longer genuinely competitive in the international sense.
The industrial engineer and the economist talk in terms of factors of production. These are men, materials, machines and money. We certainly have the men. We have people who are not only capable but people who are becoming increasingly more capable in the sense that our educational standards in this country are rising. We have the raw materials in great abundance and in most parts of Canada we have a great abundance of cheap energy. In other words, we have the men and the materials.
It may come as a surprise to some to know that in this country we also have, by and large, the machines. We are a more capitalintensive country, a more highly mechanized country, than even the United States. The recent report of the Economic Council of Canada indicated that on the average we use about 25 per cent more machinery and equipment per person employed in Canada than is the case in the United States. So we are heavily mechanized. We have the men, we have the materials and we have the machines.
What we basically lack in order to attract more money and certainly to improve our competitiveness and get our costs down are markets. We lack markets of adequate size. Often those markets can only be obtained by selling across the international border into adjoining areas of the United States.
The cure, I believe, in one industry after another is to move progressively in the direction of freer trade. Canada is by no means a free trading nation, far from it. We still erect man-made barriers against a wide range of manufactured goods. Our import duties on the average are about 20 per cent. This makes us in the eyes of many of our trading partners even more protectionist than the United States.
True, our tariff wall has been coming down. The fence which earlier generations of Canadians had built around us is not as high as it once was. Not only that, but it is being dismantled in a few important places. One such gateway was opened up last year by the present administration when it signed the Canada-United States, free trade agreement in respect of automobiles and parts. This agreement marks a major step in the right direction. It sets the stage for the uninhibited 
movement of motor vehicles and parts both ways across the international boundary line.
Canadian manufacturing plants are now free to specialize in the production of goods which they can sell not only at home in Canada but throughout the United States as well. In this way they can get their costs down. Mass production, or the economy of scale as it is sometimes called, is now on our side in respect of the automobile and parts industry. With modern factories and a cheaper Canadian dollar we can compete anywhere.
There has been considerable discussion as to the rise in prices of many categories of consumer goods. In respect of automobiles I suggest that prices over the past year have remained relatively constant. They have risen modestly in the United States. The Canada-U.S. price gap has therefore narrowed in respect of automobiles and parts. We have stabilized at least for the time being the price of automobiles to the average consumer in Canada. This is the sort of action I mean when I suggest that freer trade in respect of broad categories of industrial products will help to contain prices in this country to the benefit not only of the people who are going to produce these goods in increasing quantities but also of consumers right across the nation.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to see the present agreement expanded in the fullness of time. I should like to see it include repair parts as well. I should like to see-this is an expression of a personal opinion but I am sure that there are many other members in the house who would agree with me-the tariffs progressively removed between Canada and the United States at wholesale and retail levels, so that we eventually have something akin to price parity across the international boundary line in respect of automobiles and parts. This would mean that Canadians, at least in respect of the broad range of products produced by that industry, would be paying prices similar to those in adjoining areas of the United States.
Free trade in automobiles is, I hope, only the beginning of a process which will eventually open up the entire North American market for many of our more highly processed and a good proportion of our highly manufactured goods and services. The products of other industries will then be treated in the same way. Costs will be at a minimum, and prices to consumers will be much lower than would otherwise be the case.
March 21, 1966	COMMONS
As a westerner I am interested in highly paid jobs as well as lower prices for the consumers. But these too, can be created if our more efficient and larger resource-based industries can also tap expanding markets to the south. Doing away with U.S. tariffs in many instances will allow us to process more of our raw materials. As many hon. members know, the tariff which the United States imposes on our goods increases sharply as the degree of manufacturing increases. In other words, a penalty is imposed on jobs now in the United States; jobs, I suggest, in many industries which would otherwise exist in Canada. By reducing or eliminating tariffs in respect of these semi-processed and more highly manufactured goods we will patriate jobs to Canada. I suggest these jobs will be highly paid and are jobs which otherwise would exist only across the border in the United States.
I believe the products of our forests and our mines can be upgraded in this way. In other words, we will be processing more of our raw materials at home. This will mean more and better paid jobs for a great many Canadians.
I mentioned earlier that I was a westerner. The automobile free trade agreement, as I understand it, at the present time benefits central Canada in two important ways. It is providing many more jobs as well as a ceiling on prices. It is setting some sort of ceiling on prices for all Canada but it is not providing jobs in the rest of Canada. That is why I should like to emphasize and to advocate the opening up of negotiations in respect of the products of our forests and the products of our mines. This will create jobs in outlying areas as well as help contain prices and costs.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
What is wrong, for example, with Canada negotiating a free trade agreement in respect of pulp and paper? Newsprint and our cruder market pulps already go into the United States duty free. I would have us extend this duty free treatment to the higher valued papers and paper products, products which are valued at prices two, three and four times that of newsprint and the relatively crude pulps which we ship into the United States. By-products, including most sheet materials and wood-based chemicals, would then be saleable in the U.S.A. Not only would we be making better use of all the resources involved but we would also become manufacturers on a much larger scale. Granted, there will be opposition in some quarters. Fearing the impact of low cost imports from the United States, they will band together with a view to maintaining the status quo. But we now have an answer which even they can accept. The clue is to be found in the various measures which the government has introduced in order to offset the adverse effects of foreign competition in the automobile industry.
The owners of old and outdated plants are being helped to build new factories and switch to new lines of production. Their workers are also being retrained, in some instances with federal funds, or they are being helped to move elsewhere. Adjustment assistance, using the federal taxpayers' money, is therefore helping to ease the pain of these few unfortunate people whose shoulders would otherwise have to bear the full brunt of foreign competition.
In years gone by there was a broad philosophy expounded frequently and with great energy across this country which was taken up by most of the small "1" liberals, an idea dear to many people in western Canada. They believed that tariffs should be slashed overnight. They believed that they should not only be reduced but wiped out and done away with at once. They believed that this would cause imports to flow freely and that ultimately the standard of living would rise, not simply by increasing wages but by keeping prices at a competitive level. That was the free trade argument. Those people wanted these things to take place instantaneously and overnight.
The traditional Conservative attitude was that of creating industry at home in this country, perhaps by government assistance. Certainly that attitude favoured protection. The idea was to have a hothouse type of growth resulting in industries which eventually would be able to stand on their own feet and which would eventually be able to withstand foreign competition and thus permit the lowering of tariff barriers. These two approaches were diametrically opposed.
Today a more sophisticated approach is taken, one being used I think almost universally in western Europe and to a lesser extent in the United States. It is that of bringing about this transition over a period of years and using government funds where necessary, through research grants, through vocational training, through the retraining of workers and through grants enabling people to move from one source of employment to another, to

This is the type of industry which we ought to be developing in Canada close to the resources, close to nature. In the wood products industry we have already seen some changes. A new plant was opened recently in southern Ontario to manufacture machined wood components, not just for the Canadian market but for sale in the United States. Its annual output will shortly be worth $5 million; it expects to eventually be worth $10 million. This type of new enterprise differs from the small, highly localized inefficient plants we have had traditionally in the wood products industry. It involves a great deal of investment; it involves the training of many people and it involves the introduction of skills which we do not now possess in this country. But we must move in this direction if we are to become more competitive and set a ceiling on prices.
At this point I should like to say a word about the broader picture and about the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations. The trade expansion act gave the United States administration authority to negotiate with the united states of Europe and reach what could amount to a bilateral agreement between these two major trading blocs. Canada, in some ways, is a spectator on the sidelines. But we all hope that these negotiations will succeed, because tariff reductions as between the European Common Market and the United States will be applied to all other countries and we will find that the barriers involved in shipping our goods to the United States and Europe will be reduced if those negotiations are successful. We must, therefore, wish them well. But we must remember

So the benefits of these negotiations are not likely to be as substantial as some people hope.
We must face the possibility also that the United Kingdom may within the next two or three years become a member of the united states of Europe and find herself behind that common wall so that there will be a tariff barrier between Canada and the United Kingdom similar to that which now exists between Canada and the common market countries.

speechtext:
My point, which may be difficult to understand, is that increased trade and freer trade will lead to greater competition and this in turn will help contain prices at their present levels or even reduce them. Prices have to do with inflation. I think the argument is logical and the broader scene is also important. I say that freer trade will help us contain prices.
We on this side of the house are moving toward freer trade. Through the automobile free trade agreement we have made a tangible and I believe significant first step in the direction of freer trade in many goods and services, freer trade not only with the United States but with all other countries of the world. So we are not discriminating.
Hon. members opposite may have their solutions to this problem. I should like to know where they stand with regard to trade barriers and the possibility of increased competition during this period of high employment in Canada. This is a time of great opportunity. This is a time when we can reduce these tariff barriers. It is not possible to do so when there is high unemployment and the country is passing through a period of stagnation such as existed a few years ago. Now is the opportunity. We must seize it. I believe there is a will to move in this direction. I personally would have us move, an industry at the time, in negotiations with the United States, particularly in connection with forest and mineral products.
I would not gamble everything on the Kennedy round. I would also be prepared for the day when the United Kingdom becomes a

But I would not want us to enter this new stage in Canada's history unprepared for the changing circumstances in which we find ourselves in the world today.

Would the hon. member now permit my question? The hon. member made a carefully prepared speech on the theory of foreign trade. How does he escape the fact that Canada's adverse balance amounted to $685 million in 1965?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I do not want to escape it. It is a fact that a rapidly growing country is also a country which is mechanizing rapidly and when it has an economy like Canada's it is importing a lot of machinery and equipment. It is well known that when this country has grown rapidly it has also, for a time at least, experienced an adverse trade balance. This is a problem and it is not one which can be glossed over.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a good deal of interest to the speech made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Davis). I would have hoped it might be more apposite to the subject of the debate. In the free flow of debate I like to listen to hon. members and then try to add to what they have said or comment on the points they have made. But if I were to do so in the present case I would find myself completely off the subject because the hon. member for Coast-Capilano has certainly not restricted himself to the theme of our discussion. However, he has been putting forward his ideas and I am wondering whether he is now flying a kite to test the wind so as to see whether further steps can be taken along the lines of thinking he has outlined tonight. I have spoken about this in the past. It has not always been our experience of the Liberals that speeches made by Parliamentary Secretaries in the past expressed strictly their own ideas. I will leave the hon. member's speech as it is because it seems to me to be altogether irrelevant to the subamendment placed before us by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) as well as to the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
To deal with the subamendment, in essence it calls for a prices review board to determine

the extent to which price increases are justified and then to take steps to reduce such prices accordingly. I find myself in some difficulty on a number of points with regard to the subamendment. First, I wonder whether the federal government has the constitutional power to set up such a board along lines which would enable it to act effectively? It would appear to me that the undoubted jurisdiction of the provinces in the realm of property and civil rights would demand at least a shared jurisdiction.
That is what I suggested.

Certainly I do not believe we have any War Measures Act in existence upon the basis of which we could set up a prices review board or price control board or stabilization board such as existed in wartime, the provinces having agreed to vacate a particular field for the purpose of the prosecution of a war. But the amendment does not indicate any joint action with the provinces.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Then I have a second point. I find some uncertainty as to how it would work. Would the board have automatic powers of review or would it have to act on complaint about certain price variations in certain industries or with respect to commodities? Would it have an unfettered right to go into all forms of commodities, whether they be raw products, basic materials, or completely finished materials? Then there is the uncertainty as to how it would act. How would it enforce its decisions? Is there punitive sanction behind the authority of such a board?
There is a third point which one must consider also, namely, that in this country we are not particularly prone to accepting freely the principle of price control-and this is price control. When you start unwrapping the wrapping of this little package of a prices review board it comes down essentially to price control. That is all it means. The amendment even stipulates, "to take appropriate steps to reduce such prices accordingly." That is price control, and I do not think Canadians are prepared to accept price control in peacetime.
If one talks about price controls so far as commodities are concerned, there immediately comes into examination the question of the segments that make up the price of a commodity. There are the raw materials. Somewhere along the line they have been produced. There may have been something wrong in the pricing of the original raw

product. Is that price going to be rolled back? An integral part of all commodities is the quantum of labour that goes into them, and there we come up against the real problem of wage control. I am sure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, no more than I, does not want to institute a system of wage control or a determination of the wage scales that go into the cost of commodities.
I think the hon. member would immediately say, "We do not want wage controls". We have had to impose wage controls, with difficulty, during wartime. We have seen attempts made at wage controls in Britain in peacetime. More than one British government, more than one chancellor of the exchequer have gotten into real trouble with what they called a pay pause. Even now the present administration in Britain is having problems with its so-called unofficial wage controls. This creates industrial unrest. We have seen across the border in the United States attempts at a sort of unofficial wage control, with a lid being put on wages, which has had some rather drastic results and also some nonsensical ones. Therefore this area of uncertainty, the fact that price control is not acceptable to the Canadian people in peacetime, and the question of the constitutional right of the federal government to enter this field by itself, all give me pause and I personally find considerable difficulty in accepting the subamendment.
Let us look now at the subject of the cost of living. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition put a number of figures on the record. I may repeat some of them for the purpose of my argument. I think they bear repeating because these are the things we are worried about.
The March 11 return of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics shows that the cost of living has reached the figure of 142.1 points, an increase from 137.2 points in February 1965. In June 1963, which is the median year-I have the Canada Year Book going back to 1913, if not earlier-based on the 1949 index, the cost of living was at 137 points even. In 1962 it was 130.7; in 1961 it was 129.2 and in 1957 it was 121.9. Over the six year period from 1957 to 1963 the total increase was 11.1 points. But from June, 1963 to June 1966, which is only forecasting for a few months, the increase will have reached a total of 10 points. Therefore the increase in the cost of living in the past three years has

I find it rather odd that today both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys said it is so much easier during a period of what they called economic stagnation or depression to control the cost of living than during any other period. The cost of living index was at 113.7 in

With respect to the figures from 1957 to 1963, there was the factor of the imposition of a 3 per cent sales tax by the province of Ontario in 1962. That had quite an impact because Ontario represents one third of the country so far as population is concerned, and it had an effect on the cost of living index. [DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
What concerns the country and worries me -and I am sure hon. members opposite also are concerned-is that the government does not seem to be doing anything in respect of the most dramatic increases which hit us personally more than others, and these are in food and in housing. Let us look at food; it has gone up from 133.1 a year ago to 142.5. Housing has gone up from 140.1 to 143.1. Those are high increases. We can go back through the consumer price indices all the way down the years. For instance, in respect of food back in 1957 the index was 118.6 and in 1960 it was 122.2. In 1963 it was 130.
This evening I have been using a lot of statistics but this is the subject matter of the discussion, the movement of prices, and we can measure them only by the various indices. On many occasions this house has had motions before it with regard to the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery. Members opposite also have in this year's debate advocated the removal of that tax. It has been the contention not only of members of this house but also of many industries across the country that this has been, shall we say, one of the most potent taxes so far as the cost of living is concerned.
We can see, for instance, what has happened to the index on residential building materials over the years, and I have Dominion Bureau of Statistics records going back to 1955. The index for residential building materials stood at 298.6 in April, 1963. That was at the time of the take-over by this administration. As of December, 1965 it had reached an index figure of 346.1, or an increase of 47.5 in the period of some 32 months. We can see, going month by month through the years 1963, 1964 and 1965, the rather serious escalation every time there was the imposition of a stage of the 11 per cent sales tax.

May I indicate to hon. members that the most dramatic effect was reached in connection with lumber and its products. Lumber stood at 424.2 in April 1, 1963 and in December, 1965 reached 506.8. In other words, lumber in December, 1965 was five times as expensive as it was in the period 1935-39. Let us look at non-residential building materials, the things which go far more into the cost of producing goods and services in this country than do the costs of residential building materials.
True enough, you and I, as potential purchasers of building materials for residences, know what has happened to the price of a house, but from the point of view of being multiplied from time to time I would say that the cost of goods and services flowing from non-residential building materials has a greater effect than that which goes into residences. I should like to say that in April, 1963 the index was at 133.4 and in December of 1965 it had gone to 149.2, or an increase of 15.8. Again, lumber is the one in which there was the greatest increase.

The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), as well as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), this afternoon indicated what effect the increase in prices in Canada has had on international trade. If you do not think our international trade position is serious, I am going to refer also to the speech which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) delivered this afternoon in Toronto. I think it might be good if we put the whole of his remarks in that connection on the record. Among other things he said:
The high level of economic activity, stimulated by an extraordinarily large capital program, and coupled with shortages of labour and the difficulty of finding sufficient funds to finance all planned undertakings, will impose inflationary pressures.
This will be one of our most pressing problems as the year advances, particularly having regard to the fact that we experienced an adverse external balance on current transactions in 1965 in excess of $1 billion, and that this figure is apt to be higher in 1966. It will be recalled that the corresponding figure in 1964 was less than one-half billion dollars.
In 1961 we actually had a comfortable surplus on the commodity account but through payments and services and the tourist trade deficiency we certainly did have a

deficit in our external balance on the over all. However, it was not as bad as it was in 1957 when the deficit of the external balance on the whole, I remember, was something over $1,400 million and a good portion of that in those days was represented by a deficit in the commodity account.
It is all very well for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to say about producing goods that this government encourages by certain incentives the production of goods, but unless you are going to consume them yourself-and in this way you are selling in the domestic market-or unless these goods are sold in the external market there is no point in producing them, because there is nothing to be gained by producing goods merely to put them in warehouses to be stockpiled. This unfortunately is the position we may be driving ourselves to unless government, management and labour get together much more seriously than they have done in the past and with a much greater degree of concentration and co-operation than there has been in the past to see that we remain competitive in the international market. Otherwise Canada's industries one by one, particularly a number of the more sensitive export market industries, will wither on the vine. This is as clear as it is that the sun will rise tomorrow, because the government can go through all sorts of exercises and can provide all sorts of incentives for employment and the production of goods but unless those goods are sold the exercises will have been futile. Therefore, anything which goes to increase the cost of goods makes our position that much less competitive.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
This can be seen in relation to our wholesale price index and a number of other indices relating to commodity markets here in Canada. In the past three years we have been getting into a dangerous position. The only thing that has saved us in respect of a number of sectors of our economy has been a corresponding inflation in other countries.
We of the opposition suggest it is dangerous to have inflation in Canada, but it is widely reported in the United States at this time that the number one problem there does not relate to the war in Viet Nam but relates to the threat of inflation. We know from past experience how closely Canada's economy is related to the economy of the United States and how quickly it reflects major inflationary
Increased Cost of Living trends there. That is quite easy to understand. In 1958-59, when Canada did experience some form of economic recession, it was a reflection of the pattern set by the United States economy. In fact, it was not as severe in Canada as it was in the United States, but we know there was a relationship.
At this time we are experiencing the same sort of thing here in Canada in regard to inflation. What does this declining position in the trade picture do for us in Canada? I suggest it causes an economic slowdown. We cannot rely on one-shot, fortuitous, trading events such as the wheat deals with the Soviet Union to save our economic position. In 1963 there was a very serious threat to the value of the Canadian dollar and it was only as a result of the announced Soviet wheat deal that the pressure was removed. Were it not for that deal I am sure the situation would have been worse than that which occurred in May and June of 1962.
At this time we can read statements appearing every day in financial columns to the effect that there is some talk of pressure for devaluating the dollar because of Canada's continued deficit in international accounts. The minister has denied that there is any talk of this kind, as it is to be expected he would, but we know that pressures can build up. It may be that the United States financial community would not allow devaluation to take place because of the high stakes they have in Canada. Devaluation would be too costly and they could not allow it to happen. But this is part and parcel of the consequences of the policies advocated by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys.
For the last few minutes I have been talking about how closely our economy is tied to the economy of the United States. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano has tried to tie it even more closely so far as international trade is concerned.
Continuing inflation will create a drive for higher wages, and that is readily understood. This will create industrial unrest and dislocate economic production. As a matter of fact, it may lead to a ruinous year for some of our major industries. My colleague, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, spoke about the negative effects of inflation on persons of fixed incomes and pensions. What is the point of arranging a pension for your retirement years if the value is going to disappear unless, of course, you are not going

March 21, 1966
Increased Cost of Living to live to see it disappear? We know what has happened to people who have arranged private pensions either through government annuities or private pension schemes. We have all witnessed the continued pressure upon older citizens on old age security, pensioners and others living on the benefits of insurance programs because of a decrease in their value.
I am sure that many hon. members here have arranged insurance programs for their families and realize that the value of those schemes in the past year has dropped by 4 per cent. I do not know what the net result of the year's fiscal operations will be but if the Minister of Finance is able to come reasonably close to a decrease in the deficit forecast by his predecessor, that will to a great extent be the result of the hidden effects of inflation. Taxes based on prices such as sales tax bring in higher government revenue without any increase so far as the national product is concerned, but this is a false picture. There is an over-inflation of government revenue. I recommend that hon. members refer to the Canadian Tax Foundation observations in this regard.
The present 9 per cent level of expansion of the gross national product must reflect more this year than in the past the effects of inflation. What can we do about this situation? I do not like wage controls or price controls because I think they breed more problems than they solve. Last August the government announced a program of stretching out or cutting back on some of its expenditures. It is too bad they were not able to consult with the provinces in this regard. All of the provincial budgets this year, without exception, forecast greater expenditures on roads and building. The budget of the province of Alberta this year reflects expenditures of $682 million and that province has a population of only 1,500,000.
That is more than the budget of Canada in 1936.

A good deal of this money will be spent on education and other noncapital programs but a great deal of it will be spent on the capital expenditure side. The province of Alberta is no different in this regard from any other province. The provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia are in the same boat. That is why I feel there has been a sort of policy of drift or unwitting non-recognition of certain factors by the present administration. On the federal level it is 
turning more and more of the tax dollars over to the provinces and the Minister of Finance is handcuffed in that he cannot take steps as effectively as he could a few years ago in order to combat inflation. That is one of the consequences I have pointed out.
The federal government says it is going to apply a policy of self-denial because it feels there is some inflationary pressure. However, the provinces are free to act as they wish and they are following a course in the opposite direction. The net result is that there is no relaxation of pressure so far as building materials, labour and machinery are concerned. We are in just as bad shape in 1966 in this regard as we were in 1965. I do not think this picture is going to get better but rather it will get worse.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I still believe that the federal government and the provinces should have a conference in which they would agree on priorities of expenditure in the fields of education, health and welfare, and that we nationally must tailor our operations at the public level according to our resources in production, instead of going ahead helter-skelter and creating artificial pressures as we are now doing. I maintain that not only should those priorities be established and we should eliminate as much as possible the pressures on our resources through this, shall we say uncoordinated approach, but we should eliminate the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery. To my mind this was a hair-shirt fashioned by the former Minister of Finance. It has had a tremendous effect in creating inflationary pressure.
Where are you going to get the equivalent revenue from? Would you get it from the sales tax?
With regard to the revenues, what did the Minister of Finance do? He turned around and spent them right away.
Where are you going to get them from?

I maintain that we must have increased immigration and not necessarily immigration of those at the skilled levels equivalent to grade 10 and so on. I refer to our need of immigrants such as those who have come into this country under sponsorship and who very often have had very limited education and could not speak English or French. The great many immigrants who have come into this country since the
March 21, 1966

end of world war I and world war II have not been less productive Canadians because of these limitations. I would say that perhaps it has given them an additional spur and they have been that much more industrious. I certainly cannot agree with the report presented to us the other day which recommended that we should have less sponsored immigration. I would say we must have more and we must obtain it from these untapped sources of manpower. We must get people, bring them here and if we have to train them, for goodness sake let us get down to the job of training them in the way we want. This will give us not only an additional domestic labour market but will help in many ways. I believe this is one positive step we can advocate and this house should join in recommending it to the governments.
The house has been very tolerant with me as usual, Mr. Speaker, in allowing me to speak beyond my time. I would commend some of these points to the attention of the ministry. I do not think the ministry has been doing enough with regard to the control of inflation and for that reason I enlist the support of all members of the house in supporting the amendment that is before us.
Mr. Speaker, could I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment put forward by my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), which regrets that in view of the rising cost of living, the government has not established a prices review board to determine the extent to which price increases are justified and to take appropriate steps to reduce such prices accordingly.
At the outset I should like to draw to the attention of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who has just spoken, that in his remarks he may have overlooked several points which were made by my leader. I notice that the hon. member for Edmonton West views the subamendment with misgiving on three counts. The first was that a large share of the control of prices is provincial in scope while our subamendment proposes that the federal government should set up a prices review board.
I would point out to the hon. member for Edmonton West that our leader was very careful to point exactly to the fact that the federal government would of necessity have to take the provincial governments into consultation in setting up this board and specifying the work it should do. The federal government would be giving leadership in this field as it has in many others where jurisdiction is divided, because no province can possibly hope to cope with the question of prices within its own borders.

The second point of the hon. member had to do with the fact that prices had been controlled in wartime and that the only time we had exercised any control over prices or attempted to deal with them was in a war situation. This is true. But for many, many thousands of people across this country the present situation is very serious indeed, and the government has given lip service at least to this situation by speaking of the necessity of waging a war on poverty. I have not seen any indications of the war yet but they are talking about it. Evidently they consider the situation that many thousands of people face today to be very serious.
I would point out that the fact that we have made some attempt to deal with prices in wartime and that conditions have changed might make it quite possible to institute some kind of measures to deal with prices in a way in which we were not able to deal with them a few years ago. Conditions have changed and today the Canadian people are very anxious to see the steady rise in the cost of living stopped.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The third point which the hon. member for Edmonton West made was that he believes the Canadian people do not want control over prices. The hon. member referred to the fact that price controls would entail wage controls. I am suggesting that before any trade union can get an increase in wages today it has to go through an elaborate process of collective bargaining and a great deal of red tape.
In order to justify it.

Yes, to justify it. On the other hand, in the matter of prices there is no such machinery whatever. The way prices are raised is that the manufacturer just decides he is going to raise them and the next thing any of us know about it is when we walk into a store and find a few cents or dollars added to the prices of what we want to buy.
If we consider it a good and necessary thing to make trade unions go through a whole lot of machinery to justify wage increases before they get them, I suggest that the consumers of this country have now reached the point where they are prepared to make the same demand on the manufacturers and processors in the country. They want to see a board created before which these manufacturers will have to appear and justify the increases they are proposing to make on 
items which are necessary for the households of this country. I think that the creation of this board would be completely justified.
A great many other questions were raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West concerning how the board would function, its machinery, and so on. I listened very carefully this afternoon but I would point out that I did not hear any concrete proposal made by anyone in his party which would provide the mechanism for dealing with the question of the rising cost of living unless, of course, it was removal of the sales tax. There was no proposal whatever with regard to a program to hold down the cost of living. They just blamed the government for their inaction, and quite rightly.
In my view this party has made a proposal which would provide such a mechanism in an attempt to hold down the cost of living. We propose the idea of establishing a review board before which manufacturers would have to justify increases in their consumer prices. I have yet to hear from any other group in the house any alternative suggestion. In these days when we are hoping to do things in a responsible way I think the least people who are criticizing can do is to offer an alternative method or suggest some type of action.
We suggested that the farmers be given a fair share of the price.

That does not provide a mechanism to my way of thinking. I think more than generalities should be advanced: some sort of concrete proposal should be made.
From the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, we had a very elaborate speech about various factors of production, the need for expanding our economy, the need for mobility of manpower, the need for training and research, the need for greater trade and so on. As a speech it was perfectly all right but I do not think it went anywhere near the subject we have in mind.
The people of this country are asking for bread and they are being given the stone of government treatises. This has happened over and over again since this house opened its session. I do not think the government is prepared to grapple with the problem of rising prices. I think the government is fobbing us off with elaborate talk of trade, productivity and of all these other things
March 21, 1966

without once going near the end product of our economic system. They ought to see to it that the people of the country are enabled to provide for themselves collectively a moderate and good standard of living by their own efforts. The government should be the agent which does the planning by which this is achieved.
It just does not make sense to me to talk of an expanding economy when at the same time there is increasing distress for large sections of our people. An expanding economy with at the same time increasing distress for large sections of the community can only mean one thing. It means that too few people are getting too much of the benefits of the expanding economy and too many people are not getting enough. I do not see any other explanation. People can use all the economic jargon they like, but I do not think we can escape that conclusion.
In a period of expanding productivity and prosperity such as the present, when vast sections of our people are insecure and not so large sections are in real misery, there can be only one conclusion drawn, namely that all this affluence is not being distributed as it should. In my view the job which this government has badly neglected to do in this country is not so much related to productivity but to seeing that the results of our productivity are distributed across the country in a fair and equitable way and, particularly, that the sections of the country which need it the most are given a fair share and a moderate standard of living such as can be provided out of our resources, our machinery and our technical knowledge.
The question of steadily rising prices is one of the greatest problems to come before parliament this session. I think that tackling the problem has been far too long delayed. I have received mail, as have no doubt many other members, not only from people in my own constituency but from people clear across Canada. I have received letters from people who are desperate and keep asking what we here in Ottawa are doing. They tell us that we have good salaries and earn far more than any of them, and they ask why we cannot understand. They ask us: If, indeed, you are not too far removed from us, why can you not understand what our problems are regarding food, clothing and shelter, all the things which go to make life worth while and which we never get around to having because all our work, thought and care have to go into getting enough to eat and to wear and to

Increased Cost of Living educate our children? That is the sort of mail I receive, and I am sure the rest of the members of the house receive similar mail too.
I am going to suggest that it will not be very long before we will have to pay attention to this problem. There have been pickets of one kind or another and lobbies of one kind or another before, but I firmly expect that if we keep on turning the deaf ear and the blind eye it will not be very long before Mr. and Mrs. Consumer will come to Ottawa and picket in front of the Peace Tower. They will tell us that they are sick and tired of hearing us all moaning about the cost of living but doing nothing about it. I think it is time we grappled with the problem. When I say "we" I mean the government, which has the ultimate responsibility for coming to grips with the question and finding policies to meet the situation.
It is no good for the government to tell us, as we have been told over and over again, that they must wait for the Economic Council to make its report at the end of the year before they can find out what kind of measures they will take. That is one answer we have been given.
Another answer I was given when I asked a question on the orders of the day was that the government feels its present economic and other policies are enough to ensure that the cost of living will not keep rising. Today we were told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp): "Just wait till I bring the budget down and perhaps you will find something there to deal with cost of living". I want to suggest that this is not good enough for the people of this country today.
What are the plain facts? The cost of living has gone up 3i per cent over the last 12 months. The February price index, the latest one we have, shows that prices are up on nearly everything-clothing, housing, household utilities of all kinds. The most alarming increase has been in the price of food. When you come down to food, Mr. Speaker, you get down to rock bottom. You get down to the only item which is regarded as flexible for budgetary purposes, because the other items carry a fixed cost and have to be met.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The foods which are particularly affected are listed in the February index, as they were in the January index, and comprise butter and other fats, meat, fish and poultry and vegetables. They are the foods which are

March 21, 1966
Increased Cost of Living absolutely essential for building healthy bodies and creating strong nerves and healthy minds. The women of this country have been propagandized by the government for so long now that they know these are the foods necessary to create good bodies, strong nerves and healthy minds. Now they are no longer able to buy those things and they cannot understand why the government they have elected, and the members they have elected to this house do not see to it that they are able to buy the foods that their families and husbands need to maintain good health.
I say that it is alarming to see food prices steadily going up. Food price increases hit us all but they do not hit us all evenly. You cannot look at people too much as if they are statistics in columns in a book. People are not statistics in books; they are all individuals and each one of their cases is different. Pressures on different people do not hit them the same way. The price rise in an item which merely irritates a person earning $10,000 a year may be a very serious thing for the worker with a family who earns perhaps $50 a week, and it may be catastrophic to a veteran or to somebody on an old age pension or some other kind of fixed income.
We do not realize that these rises in the price of foods are as serious as they are. Price rises strike at the very well-being of Canadian families. They particularly attack families in low and fixed income groups. I do not care, Mr. Speaker, how much we have in the way of automobiles, pulp and paper and all the other great things of our economy if we cannot find ways and means of feeding our families across this country. If we are not feeding them, we are not doing our job as members of parliament.
All these other things we have are simply wasted and useless unless the people of this country can have access to the foods they need. I think of thousands of families, not necessarily families in British Columbia but self-respecting families everywhere, most of them paying their own way, who are finding it harder and harder to make their pay cheques go around to buy the things they as families need to make a modern standard of living possible. They have every right to a modern standard of living.
I think of a young couple newly married who are trying very hard to set aside a little bit for the family they hope to raise, who are buying furniture on time, as are other people. Far from getting ahead, they are finding that

the rising cost of living is robbing them even of the little they have been able to put aside; the rising cost of living is destroying the plans they have been making. They find that their future is dwindling and shrivelling like something being burned up in a fire. They are filled with despair because while they are doing everything they can in the right way the rising cost of living is depriving them of the fruits of their labour.
I 'think of Mr. and Mrs. M. and their five children. Mrs. M. knows all about the things that children need to have. She is a good, faithful and intelligent woman. She knows the need for a balanced diet and she cannot get it for her children any more. I have seen this woman in my own riding and others like her in other parts of British Columbia going into stores to shop, hoping to pick up those things which they bought the previous week and trying to buy perhaps one or two little treats for the family but finding that the price has risen two or three cents on this product, perhaps five cents on something else and a few cents on something else. I have seen these women come out sad and feeling very apprehensive about what is going to happen the next time they go shopping.
Things are made much worse when one realizes that these women cannot buy the food needed for the health of their children. I am not talking only of British Columbia. Here is a letter from a woman in London, Ontario:
In this area over the last three months there has been an increase in milk, bread, butter, meat, fruit, vegetables, newspapers and bus transportation and not long before-hydro, water and telephone rates. It is pathetic to see our older citizens walk long distances in cold weather because they can no longer afford transportation.
Here is a letter from New Brunswick:
The (Federal) Government granted a ten dollar a month raise in the old age pension some time ago and all of us got our rent raised $10 a month immediately so you can see that raise did not go far . . . Now the Provincial government is raising the sales tax to 6% from 3% on April 1st.
That is why our leader proposed that Ottawa should take the lead in calling the provincial governments together to consider how to establish a price review board. The provincial governments are levying their own taxes and those taxes are attacking the same family budget that high prices are attacking and lessening the value of the same family dollar.
Therefore we have to make a concerted attack on this sort of thing and this is the only place from which a concerted, well
March 21, 1966

directed attack can come. All across the country millions of families are waiting to see what the government is going to do.
Here is a letter from a mother of a family in Newfoundland who has a sick husband:
Prices are preposterous and it's time someone did something about them. My sick husband needs a special diet, our son needs a high protein bodybuilding diet, our other children also need bodybuilding foods. Needless to say there is never enough to provide us with all this.
I want to say that all across Canada tonight these families are watching and waiting hopefully to see what if anything this government is going to do. They do not figure that a government that was just elected last fall has lost steam and they believe it still wants to do something. These people still hope that something is going to come out of Ottawa. However, they are not going to continue to believe that. They are not going to maintain that faith if there is no relief on the horizon.
What is the government doing about the rise in cost of living? This afternoon we heard the Minister of Finance say that now we are in a period of prosperity which is remarkable not only for being one of the greatest but also one of the most prolonged. That is simply not true for thousands of people in Canada today. They are living in insecurity and poverty and they need help badly.
What is the sense of having a society that is part affluent and part poor? In fact, those of us who are affluent will not long keep our affluence if we are going to permit poverty to exist. I say that instead of chasing all over Europe and the rest of the world looking for markets it is time we looked at the home market with a view to building up that market here in this country. Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock.

EXPO '67-REFUSAL OF PERMISSION TO RECORD R.C.M.P. BAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that this matter which I raised last Thursday and today is a very serious one that really affects the interests of Canadians. I think it is depressing that an international union with headquarters in New York should dictate whether or not a

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion recording should be made of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police band at Expo '67, a band that is paid for by the taxpayers of this country.
Because the R.C.M.P. band members do not belong to a union Canadians are not going to be allowed to buy recordings of a tattoo by that band at Expo '67. This is a cultural project. It seems to me a very discriminatory practice that the American Federation of Musicians would not allow a Toronto recording producer, or for that matter any recording producer, to make records of the tattoo which is going to be presented by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police band. It is all the more discriminatory when such permission has been granted by this union to the U.S. army, air force, navy and marine corps bands whose members are also non-union and when their performances have also been cultural projects. But when the purpose of the R.C.M.P. tattoo is also cultural and a part of Canada's centennial celebration this union will not allow the R.C.M.P. band to make recordings.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I do not wish to speak at great length on this matter, but I think this is a ridiculous situation. The R.C.M.P. band is supposed to be one of the finest in our country and I think it is incumbent upon the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), whom I see in the house, to intervene in all possible ways so as to obtain permission from the union for the recording to be made. If all these approaches fail I suggest that the government provide facilities through the C.B.C. or the National Film Board or any other crown agency to have recordings made of this band.
As one who has at times acted on behalf of international unions I think this is a disgraceful situation. It is completely discriminatory to allow United States bands to be recorded but not a Canadian band. This band has not even been allowed to perform at the Canadian National Exhibition because of this discriminatory practice and I suggest that the Secretary of State make every intervention possible and adopt every means open to the government to persuade the union to give its permission to have this performance recorded or else to allow crown agency facilities to be used for this worth-while project.

Incidentally, I do intend to disprove categorically that part of the item of the Toronto Daily Star to the effect that the report promised by the Prime Minister in his secretary's letter dated November 30, 1965, in reply to that of Mr. Warriner, dated November 17, 1965, had not yet been provided on March 11, 1966. maintopic: EXPO '67-REFUSAL OF PERMISSION TO RECORD R.C.M.P. BAND
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I am not concerned with an article in the Toronto Star of which I have no knowledge. I am concerned only with what action is to be taken with respect to recordings of this particular band. I am not concerned about the producer named by the Parliamentary Secretary but about what action is to be taken.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: EXPO '67-REFUSAL OF PERMISSION TO RECORD R.C.M.P. BAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the suggestion of the hon. member for Hamilton West to the effect that there is discrimination-and it is the question put to the Secretary of State, by the Vice President of the American Federation of Musicians in refusing the request by Arc Sound Limited- is easily given.
The house and the hon. member should know that all agreements entered into by the
musicians' union and the recording companies, provide that companies may not record any musician who is not a member of the union, in this case the American Federation of Musicians.
Now the R.C.M.P. band are not members of the union and, consequently, there is no cause to cry foul play and discrimination.
Furthermore, since the hon. member and Mr. Warriner seem to insist upon what they call the ridicule of a Canadian band being dominated by a foreign labour organization, I may add that a similar proviso could be included in the regulations of a Canadian union and this company or any other would not have the right to record the R.C.M.P. band.
Mr. Warriner claims it would cost $40,000 in musicians' fees and suggests that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) find the funds to meet this obligation. Having presented his case to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), he was told that it would not be advisable to take this amount from public funds to record the music of a military band for purely commercial purposes. The same reply was given by the Department of Justice who has jurisdiction over the R.C.M.P., and by the Centennial Commission.
However, the R.C.M.P. has no objection to having the music of its band recorded for commercial purposes, but since this would be a competitive engagement, the recording company would have to obtain permission from the American Federation of Musicians and provide the funds or find an acceptable sponsor.
